analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps to $7.25 an hour and extends it to the Northern Mariana Islands.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill: it sat in a subcommittee of the Education and Workforce Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress, despite 144 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal minimum wage had been stuck at $5.15 an hour since 1997. This bill would have raised it in three steps to $5.85, then $6.55, then $7.25 over about two years. It would also have ended the Northern Mariana Islands' special exemption from federal wage law, phasing the island's roughly $3.05 minimum up to the federal level. Rep. George Miller introduced it with 144 cosponsors, but the Republican-run House committee sent it to a subcommittee and never brought it to a vote, and the Congress ended in January 2007 with the bill dead.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of workers paid at or near the federal minimum, concentrated in restaurants, retail, hotels, and home care, plus workers in the Northern Mariana Islands who were outside federal wage law entirely.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers earning at or near $5.15 an hour

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum wage in three steps: $5.85 beginning 60 days after enactment, $6.55 a year later, and $7.25 a year after that, the first increase since 1997.

Extends federal minimum wage law to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, which had been exempt, with the local minimum phased up by 50 cents every six months until it equals the federal wage.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of minimum-wage workers, especially small restaurants, retailers, and hotels that pay wages at or near the floor, and the Northern Mariana Islands' garment industry, which relied on the exemption.
analysis.who_pays_short: Small low-wage employers and island garment makers

drawbacks.text: Raising the wage floor increases labor costs most for small restaurants, retailers, and nonprofits that already pay near minimum wage and cannot pass costs on easily; a stronger wage floor also means higher prices in low-wage service industries.

The Northern Mariana Islands change, though phased, would have been steep for the island economy: the local minimum would rise from about $3.05 to the federal $7.25, a challenge for an economy built on a large garment sector paying below federal wages.

A minimum wage raise is not well targeted to family need: it raises pay for some teenagers and second earners in non-poor households, while adults who cannot find work or work limited hours see nothing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: millions of the lowest-paid workers get a raise, and their employers absorb higher costs. The evidence on job losses from modest minimum wage increases is mixed, but the cost to small businesses in low-wage industries is real and concentrated. The CNMI provision ends a genuine anomaly, a U.S. jurisdiction outside federal wage law, and phases the change so island employers are not hit all at once. On balance the bill is a modest, conventional wage increase whose main flaw is that it never got a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The House's Republican leadership never allowed a vote: the bill was referred to the Education and Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller of California introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2005 on May 18, 2005, with 144 cosponsors.
Of the 144 cosponsors, 141 were House Democrats, 2 were Republicans, and 1 was an Independent, meaning nearly the whole Democratic caucus backed the bill.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on May 18, 2005, and on June 22 was referred further to its Subcommittee on Workforce Protections.

The bill was never reported out of committee and never received a floor vote; the only further entries in its action history are three rounds of sponsor introductory remarks in 2005 and 2006, and the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 with the wage unchanged at $5.15.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of minimum-wage workers were better off, since the federal wage stayed at $5.15 for two more years, and the Northern Mariana Islands kept its exemption and its sub-federal wage floor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers and island garment makers

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: U.S. Representative (CA-7), senior Democrat on the Education and Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and repeatedly gave floor remarks pressing for action on it through 2005 and 2006.

for.name: 141 of 201 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, along with 1 Independent and 2 Republicans.

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Speaker Dennis Hastert
against.what_they_did: Never brought a minimum wage increase to the House floor for a vote during the 109th Congress.

against.name: Jack Abramoff and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands' garment industry
against.role: Lobbyists for the Northern Mariana Islands government and garment manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Lobbied for years to keep the islands exempt from federal wage law, the exemption this bill would have ended; the arrangement became the subject of a Senate investigation and Abramoff's guilty plea in 2006.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly unanimous among Democrats: 141 of 144 cosponsors were House Democrats, with 2 Republicans and 1 Independent, while the Republican-run House never scheduled the bill for action.

industries.industry: Low-wage service employers (restaurants, retail, hotels, home care)
industries.note: These employers pay most of the nation's minimum-wage workers, so the bill raises their labor costs in exchange for their workers getting a raise. Keeping the floor at $5.15 was worth an estimated several billion dollars a year to them, which is why business lobbies opposed wage increases and the House majority left the bill unvoted.

The bill ends the islands' exemption from federal wage law and phases their roughly $3.05 minimum up to $7.25, removing the sub-federal wages that underpinned the islands' garment manufacturing. The industry had long lobbied to preserve that exemption.
